plain: The boat-shaped carpal bone on the thumb side of the proximal row. It bridges the two rows of carpal bones, so almost every wrist movement passes through it.
detail: Proximal row, lateral-most. Articulates with the radius, lunate, capitate, trapezium and trapezoid. Its tubercle is palpable at the base of the thenar eminence and forms the lateral wall of the carpal tunnel.
clinical: The most commonly fractured carpal bone, typically from a fall on the outstretched hand. Its blood supply enters distally and runs backwards, so a fracture across the waist can cut off the proximal fragment's supply and cause avascular necrosis. Tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox is the classic sign, and early X-rays are often normal.

plain: The moon-shaped carpal bone sitting in the middle of the proximal row, directly under the radius.
detail: Proximal row, between the scaphoid and triquetrum. Its deep concave distal surface cups the head of the capitate.
clinical: The most commonly dislocated carpal bone. A dislocated lunate is pushed forward into the carpal tunnel and can compress the median nerve. Avascular necrosis of the lunate is called Kienböck disease.

plain: The three-cornered carpal bone on the little-finger side of the proximal row.
detail: Articulates with the lunate, pisiform and hamate. It does not touch the radius directly — an articular disc separates it from the ulna.
clinical: The second most commonly fractured carpal bone, usually a chip off its dorsal surface.

plain: A pea-sized bone sitting on the front of the triquetrum. It is a sesamoid bone — it formed inside a tendon rather than as part of the carpal skeleton proper.
detail: Lies within the tendon of flexor carpi ulnaris. Easily felt at the base of the hypothenar eminence. Forms the medial boundary of the carpal tunnel along with the hook of the hamate.
clinical: The ulnar nerve and artery pass just lateral to it, through Guyon's canal. Prolonged pressure here — classically from cycling handlebars — causes ulnar nerve symptoms in the hand.

plain: The distal-row carpal bone at the base of the thumb. Its saddle-shaped joint with the thumb metacarpal is what lets the human thumb oppose.
detail: Articulates with the scaphoid, trapezoid, and the 1st and 2nd metacarpals. The saddle (sellar) first carpometacarpal joint permits flexion, extension, abduction, adduction and — uniquely — opposition.
clinical: Osteoarthritis of the first carpometacarpal joint is very common, especially in older women, and causes pain at the thumb base when gripping or pinching.

plain: The smallest bone of the distal carpal row, wedged between the trapezium and the capitate at the base of the index finger.
detail: Articulates with the scaphoid, trapezium, capitate and the 2nd metacarpal. Its wedge shape makes it very stable.
clinical: Rarely injured in isolation precisely because it is so well protected.

plain: The largest carpal bone, sitting in the centre of the wrist. Its rounded head fits into the socket formed by the scaphoid and lunate.
detail: Distal row, central. Articulates with the scaphoid, lunate, trapezoid, hamate and the 2nd, 3rd and 4th metacarpals. It is the first carpal bone to ossify.
clinical: Because it sits at the centre of the wrist, the capitate is the axis around which the carpus moves; injuries here disturb wrist mechanics broadly.

plain: The wedge-shaped carpal bone on the little-finger side of the distal row. It carries a hook on its palmar surface.
detail: The hook of the hamate (hamulus) forms the medial wall of the carpal tunnel and the lateral wall of Guyon's canal. Articulates with the lunate, triquetrum, capitate and the 4th and 5th metacarpals.
clinical: Fracture of the hook of the hamate happens in racquet and club sports from the grip pressing into the palm. The deep branch of the ulnar nerve curves right around the hook and can be injured with it.

plain: The forearm bone on the thumb side. It is the bone that actually carries the wrist — the hand hangs from the radius, not the ulna.
detail: Its distal end articulates with the scaphoid and lunate at the radiocarpal joint, and with the ulnar head at the distal radio-ulnar joint. The radial styloid extends further distally than the ulnar styloid.
clinical: Colles fracture — a distal radius fracture with dorsal displacement — is the commonest fracture in adults over 50, from falling on an outstretched hand. It gives the classic 'dinner fork' deformity.

plain: The forearm bone on the little-finger side. At the wrist it is separated from the carpal bones by an articular disc, so it does not form part of the wrist joint proper.
detail: The distal ulna carries the head and the styloid process. The triangular fibrocartilage complex separates it from the triquetrum.
clinical: The ulnar styloid is often avulsed alongside a Colles fracture.

plain: The metacarpal of the thumb. It is shorter and stouter than the others, and it is rotated about 90° relative to them — which is why the thumb faces the other fingers.
detail: Its base forms the saddle joint with the trapezium. Unlike the other metacarpals, its epiphysis is at the base, not the head.
clinical: A Bennett fracture is an intra-articular fracture-dislocation of its base; adductor pollicis pulls the shaft while the small proximal fragment stays put.

plain: The metacarpal of the little finger, on the outer edge of the palm.
detail: Its base articulates with the hamate. It has more mobility at its carpometacarpal joint than the 2nd and 3rd, which lets the palm cup.
clinical: A 'boxer's fracture' is a fracture of its neck, from punching with a closed fist. The head tilts into the palm.

plain: The nerve that runs down the middle of the forearm and enters the hand through the carpal tunnel. It supplies most of the muscles that let you pinch and grip, and sensation to the thumb side of the palm.
detail: Formed from the lateral and medial cords of the brachial plexus (C6–T1). In the hand it supplies the thenar muscles (via the recurrent branch) and the 1st and 2nd lumbricals, plus skin over the lateral three and a half digits on the palmar side.
clinical: Compression inside the carpal tunnel causes carpal tunnel syndrome — tingling and numbness in the thumb, index and middle fingers, worse at night, with thenar wasting if long-standing. Note that the palmar cutaneous branch leaves before the tunnel, so the central palm keeps its sensation.

en: Recurrent branch of the median nerve
plain: A short branch that loops back from the median nerve as soon as it leaves the carpal tunnel, to supply the thumb muscles.
detail: Supplies abductor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis and the superficial head of flexor pollicis brevis.
clinical: It lies very superficially just distal to the flexor retinaculum, so a shallow laceration of the palm can divide it and abolish opposition of the thumb — hence its nickname among surgeons.

plain: The nerve on the little-finger side of the hand. It supplies almost all the small muscles inside the hand, so it controls fine finger movements.
detail: From the medial cord of the brachial plexus (C8–T1). Enters the hand through Guyon's canal, superficial to the flexor retinaculum, alongside the ulnar artery. Supplies the hypothenar muscles, all interossei, the 3rd and 4th lumbricals, adductor pollicis and the deep head of flexor pollicis brevis.
clinical: Injury produces a 'claw hand' — the ring and little fingers hyperextend at the metacarpophalangeal joints and flex at the interphalangeal joints, because the interossei and lumbricals are paralysed. Froment's sign tests adductor pollicis.

en: Deep branch of the ulnar nerve
plain: The purely motor branch of the ulnar nerve. It dives deep into the palm and curves across it, supplying almost all the small muscles of the hand.
detail: Passes between abductor digiti minimi and flexor digiti minimi brevis, hooks around the hook of the hamate, then runs laterally with the deep palmar arch to end in adductor pollicis.
clinical: Because it winds round the hook of the hamate, a fractured hook or chronic pressure on the palm can paralyse the intrinsic muscles while sensation stays completely normal.

plain: The deeper of the two arterial loops in the palm, formed mainly by the radial artery. It lies about a finger's breadth proximal to the superficial arch.
detail: Formed by the terminal part of the radial artery joining the deep palmar branch of the ulnar artery. Lies on the bases of the metacarpals, deep to the long flexor tendons. Gives off the palmar metacarpal arteries.
clinical: The two palmar arches anastomose freely, which is why the hand tolerates loss of either the radial or ulnar artery. Allen's test checks this before taking a radial artery graft or cannulating it.

plain: The main artery of the thumb, branching from the radial artery as it enters the palm.
detail: Arises from the radial artery as it turns medially between the heads of the first dorsal interosseous, then divides into two proper palmar digital arteries for the sides of the thumb.

plain: An artery running down the front of the interosseous membrane between the radius and ulna, supplying the deep forearm muscles.
detail: A branch of the common interosseous artery from the ulnar artery. Accompanies the anterior interosseous nerve and ends by piercing the interosseous membrane to join the dorsal carpal arch.

plain: The most superficial thenar muscle. It pulls the thumb away from the palm, straight out at right angles.
detail: From the flexor retinaculum, scaphoid tubercle and trapezium, to the lateral side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the thumb. Supplied by the recurrent branch of the median nerve.
clinical: This is the muscle tested when you ask a patient to raise the thumb vertically against resistance — the standard bedside test for median nerve function in carpal tunnel syndrome. Wasting of the thenar eminence is mostly wasting of this muscle.

plain: A fan-shaped muscle deep in the palm that pulls the thumb back towards the index finger — the movement you use to grip a sheet of paper.
detail: Two heads: transverse from the shaft of the 3rd metacarpal, oblique from the capitate and bases of the 2nd and 3rd metacarpals. Inserts into the medial side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the thumb. Supplied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve.
clinical: Froment's sign: ask the patient to grip paper between thumb and index finger. If adductor pollicis is paralysed by an ulnar nerve lesion, they compensate by flexing the thumb's interphalangeal joint using flexor pollicis longus (median nerve).

plain: The most superficial hypothenar muscle, along the outer edge of the palm. It spreads the little finger away from the others.
detail: From the pisiform and the tendon of flexor carpi ulnaris to the medial side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the little finger. Supplied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve.

plain: A long muscle coming from the back of the forearm to the base of the thumb. Its tendon forms the front edge of the anatomical snuffbox.
detail: From the posterior surfaces of the radius, ulna and interosseous membrane to the base of the 1st metacarpal. Supplied by the posterior interosseous nerve.
clinical: Its tendon shares a sheath with extensor pollicis brevis at the radial styloid. Inflammation of that shared sheath is de Quervain's tenosynovitis, tested with Finkelstein's test.

plain: The bulky muscle you can feel in the web between thumb and index finger. Dorsal interossei ABduct the fingers away from the middle finger.
detail: Bipennate, arising from the adjacent sides of the 1st and 2nd metacarpals, inserting into the lateral side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the index finger. Supplied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve.
clinical: Wasting of the first web space is the earliest visible sign of an ulnar nerve lesion, because this muscle is large and superficial. Remember DAB and PAD: Dorsal ABduct, Palmar ADduct.

plain: A small worm-shaped muscle that runs from a flexor tendon in the palm to the back of the index finger. Lumbricals bend the knuckle while straightening the finger — the position you hold a book in.
detail: Arises from the lateral side of the flexor digitorum profundus tendon to the index finger and inserts into the radial side of its extensor expansion. Unusually, it takes origin from a tendon rather than bone. The 1st and 2nd lumbricals are supplied by the median nerve, the 3rd and 4th by the ulnar nerve.
clinical: That split nerve supply is why an ulnar nerve lesion claws only the ring and little fingers — the index and middle fingers keep their median-supplied lumbricals.

plain: A tough triangular sheet of fibrous tissue just under the skin of the palm. It anchors the skin so the palm can grip without sliding.
detail: Continuous with the flexor retinaculum and the tendon of palmaris longus proximally; distally it splits into four slips that run to the fingers and blend with the fibrous flexor sheaths.
clinical: Progressive thickening and contracture of this sheet is Dupuytren's contracture, which pulls the ring and little fingers into permanent flexion.

plain: A long muscle running along the thumb side of the forearm. Despite being in the extensor compartment, it bends the elbow.
detail: From the lateral supracondylar ridge of the humerus to the base of the radial styloid process. Supplied by the radial nerve — one of the few flexors it supplies.
clinical: Strongest when the forearm is midway between pronation and supination, which is why it stands out when you lift something with your thumb pointing up.

plain: One of the muscles that cocks the wrist backwards and tilts it towards the thumb.
detail: From the lateral supracondylar ridge of the humerus to the base of the 2nd metacarpal, dorsally. Supplied by the radial nerve directly, before it divides.
clinical: Because it is supplied above the division of the radial nerve, wrist extension is partly preserved in a posterior interosseous nerve palsy — unlike a true radial nerve injury in the spiral groove, which gives complete wrist drop.

plain: A slender muscle that straightens the little finger on its own.
detail: From the common extensor origin on the lateral epicondyle to the extensor expansion of the little finger. Supplied by the posterior interosseous nerve.

plain: Slippery fluid-filled tubes wrapped around the finger flexor tendons so they glide freely inside their fibrous tunnels.
detail: The sheaths of the index, middle and ring fingers are separate and end at the level of the metacarpal heads. The little finger's sheath is usually continuous with the common flexor sheath (ulnar bursa), and the thumb's with the radial bursa.
clinical: That continuity matters: infection in the little finger or thumb can track proximally into the palm and forearm, whereas infection in the other fingers stays local. This is why suppurative tenosynovitis is a surgical emergency.
